title: Anthropic quietly pitches its own AI safety bill to lawmakers
source_used: Politico (first reporter), read as relayed by Reuters on CNA and by Bloomberg on The Edge Malaysia
key_facts: Politico reported on Friday 16 Oct 2026, citing three people with knowledge of the effort, that Anthropic representatives have quietly pitched Capitol Hill lawmakers on a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security.

Under the draft the government could block a model's release or use only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people.
The risk must come from creating or releasing a biological weapon, the model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack.

Independent evaluators, registered with the Commerce Department, would periodically assess labs and their frontier models, and must report an imminent enumerated risk to Commerce within 72 hours; labs could pay them if payment is not tied to the outcome.

Commerce could ask a federal judge to halt a model; the language bars any other US department, agency or officer from suspending development, deployment or internal use, and a judge at the District Court for the District of Columbia could order a suspension.
The proposal would also override certain state laws, such as California's, according to the Reuters write-up of the report.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects the company's Advanced AI Framework, advocated to federal and state lawmakers since June, and requires testing, public transparency about findings and independent evaluation.
Congress has not passed a federal AI law and is out of session until after the midterm elections; the Trump administration has relied on voluntary industry pledges.
quote_evidence: This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic's Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June.

The proposal suggests the government could block the release of an AI model if it's determined to imminently risk killing or injuring more than 50 people or causing more than US$1 billion (RM4.08 billion) in damages, according to Politico, which first reported on the bill.
The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California.
why_it_matters_hint: A leading AI lab has written the first concrete federal bill text for limiting dangerous AI models, with high thresholds and limits on states and other agencies that lawmakers may contest.
